PCA cannot tell structure from redundancy and noise
Stimuli confine neural population activity to low-dimensional subspaces, usually inferred
with principal component analysis (PCA). But recordings also carry nuisance covariance
that is present even without a stimulus:
Redundancy: neurons co-fluctuate during spontaneous activity [4]

Measure variance relative to explicit baselines
bPCA compares the test data with a redundancy baseline, in which the system varies without
the constraint, and a noise baseline, which captures the measurement alone.
bPCA solves the generalized eigenvalue problem
Each eigenvalue λ is the test variance above the noise
floor, in units of the redundancy baseline (c). With an

tspan.tspan: We decoded the direction of drifting gratings (0°, 45°, 90° or 135°; 75 trials each) from
Neuropixels recordings of mouse visual cortex (Allen Visual Coding, Functional Connectivity
set [5]; 23 sessions; 18 male and 5 female mice), pooling all visual cortical units.

text.tspan: Test data: trial-mean firing rates during gratings
Redundancy baseline: spontaneous activity, cut into trial-length windows
Noise baseline: measurement error of each unit's rate, from spontaneous activity (below)

With spontaneous activity as the redundancy baseline, bPCA concentrates stimulus
information into its leading components, cutting the two-component decoding error by 22°
